_readme: Approved changes to the AI prompt files. tests/prompt-guard.test.js undoes these edits and checks the result is byte-for-byte the original prompt (baselineSha256). Any other change to a prompt fails the test. Add an entry here only for a change the owner asked for.

edits.why: Location Note removed from the profile at the owner's request: the AI works out the commute from the Address and the job location.
edits.before: If the role is local to where the candidate lives, reference proximity naturally where it adds genuine value
edits.after: If the role is local to where the candidate lives, reference proximity naturally where it adds genuine value. Work out whether it is local yourself: compare the candidate's Address in the content bank's personal details with the work location in the JD, and estimate the usual travel time from the candidate's suburb to that location from your own knowledge of the area. If it is about 30 minutes or less, you may mention it once in the professional summary, as an approximate figure with the suburb and state only (e.g. "based in Albury, NSW, about 10 minutes from the site"). Never write the street address. Always say "about" or "around", because it is an estimate. If you are unsure of the location or the travel time, the role is fully remote, or the commute is long, leave proximity out, and never invent a willingness to relocate.

edits.why: New Position Description field per role; tells the AI how role descriptions and bullet lines are read so nothing is counted twice. Updated: "Link:" lines belong to the bullet above. Updated at the owner's request: the description carries the same weight as the bullets, for every role.
edits.before: - [EXPERIENCE]: for each role, a header line "### <Job Title> | <Dates>", optionally followed by " | [Responsibilities](url)" or " | [Website](url)" as a third field. Next line: the organisation and location, optionally followed by " | [Milestones](url)". If the role absorbed an earlier title, add a line starting "Previously: <earlier title and dates>". Then 3-6 achievement bullets each starting with "- ". Separate roles with one blank line. Reverse chronological. Every bullet starts with a past-tense action verb and quantifies outcomes where possible.

- In the content bank, a role's "Description:" line describes the position (its purpose, scope and team) and may hold the role's strongest achievement. Give it the same importance as the role's bullets: use it as a bullet, merge it into one, or use it to frame the role, whichever best serves the JD. Never state the same point twice, whether it comes from the description or a bullet. Every other line under a role, after its header lines, is one separate responsibility or achievement (except "Link:" lines, which belong to the bullet just above them): count and use each line once.

edits.why: Usage Notes removed from the profile at the owner's request: the candidate no longer writes a role-to-story map, so the prompt tells the AI to build that mapping itself from the whole content bank against the job description.
edits.before: The content bank drives this selection. Each entry in its STORY BANK carries a "Best used for:" line, and its USAGE NOTES section maps role types to the stories that suit them. Read both before choosing. Where they cover the role you are writing for, follow them — they are the candidate's own judgement about which evidence is strongest.
edits.after:
Do this mapping yourself, from the whole content bank. There is no pre-written list of which stories suit which roles, so build one for this job before you write anything:

1. From the JD, list its five to eight core requirements, most important first: the tasks the person will spend most of their time on, the hardest part of the job, and the essential selection criteria.
2. For each requirement, search the entire content bank for evidence: every role's description and bullets (not only the most recent role), every STORY BANK entry, Personal Projects, Skills, Certifications, Education, Awards and Achievements, including any links attached to an item.
3. Rank the evidence for each requirement. Direct proof of the same task beats transferable proof. A quantified outcome beats an unquantified one. Recent beats old. Paid work beats a side project, unless the side project is the closer match. A story's "Best used for:" line is only the candidate's hint; the JD decides.
4. Build the CV from the top of each ranking: the summary's proof points, the bullets you keep for each role, and the skills you list. Drop evidence that matches no requirement, and do not use the same proof point in more than two places.
5. If a core requirement has no evidence in the content bank, never imply it is met. Leave it out, and name it as a gap in your tailoring note.

Keep every claim tied to the role, timeframe and wording it comes from in the content bank, and never stretch a fact: do not widen a timeframe (something done at one employer is not "for six years"), add a tool, method or detail the content bank does not name, or turn a single example into a general habit.
Before delivering, proofread for real errors only: a pronoun with nothing to match, a missing "that" or "in" that makes a line hard to follow, a verb that does not agree with its subject, a phrase that could attach to the wrong thing, or an abbreviation not spelled out the first time. Fix those and leave the wording, tone and sentence length otherwise as they are.

edits.after:
- Does any phrase in the introduction sound constructed rather than said? If yes, replace it with a plain fact.
- Is anything grammatically wrong? Fix real errors only: a pronoun with nothing to match (such as "them" after a singular noun), a missing "that" or "in" that makes a sentence hard to follow, a verb that does not agree with its subject, a trailing phrase that could attach to the wrong thing, or an abbreviation not spelled out the first time. Leave deliberate short sentences, fragments and informal phrasing exactly as they are, and never change a line this prompt tells you to keep word for word.
